topic: Brunei split in two and six more cut-off lands, ending with India's Tin Bigha Corridor
hook: Your old drive across Brunei meant crossing Malaysia twice, with passport stamps, just to reach your own country.
title: 7 Maps That Look Fake But Are Real
description:
Brunei is cut in two by Malaysia, The Gambia is a ribbon inside Senegal, and Bangladeshi villages sit inside India behind a gate. This countdown shows seven real, odd-shaped places on simple animated maps, ending with India's Tin Bigha Corridor. Every fact is true, and the strangest one is on India's own border.

#geography #borders #facts
comment_prompt: Which of the seven would you visit first?

scenes.narration: Your old drive across Brunei meant crossing Malaysia twice, with passport stamps, just to reach your own country.
scenes.headline: Two Stamps, One Country

scenes.narration: Today, seven places where a country is cut off from its own land. Every single one is real.
scenes.headline: Seven Real Maps

scenes.narration: By the end, you will see a small strip of India with a gate, built for another country's citizens.
scenes.headline: A Gate In India

scenes.narration: Each stop comes with a simple map, so you can see the odd shape yourself.
scenes.headline: See The Shape

scenes.narration: So we start at number seven, and count down to the strangest border in all of India.
scenes.headline: The Countdown

scenes.narration: Number seven. Brunei, a small oil-rich country on the island of Borneo, is cut into two separate pieces.
scenes.headline: Brunei Split In Two

scenes.narration: Look at the map. The big western part holds the capital, Bandar Seri Begawan, and a smaller eastern part called Temburong floats alone.
scenes.headline: Two Separate Pieces

scenes.narration: Between them sits Limbang, a district of Malaysia's state of Sarawak. It cuts Brunei neatly in two.
scenes.headline: Limbang Cuts Through

scenes.narration: Sarawak's ruler annexed Limbang in 1890, so this split on the map is more than a century old.
scenes.headline: Split Since 1890

scenes.narration: Brunei also claimed Limbang for a long time, though in 2009 the two countries settled the matter.
scenes.headline: The Claim Ends

scenes.narration: Temburong is mostly green rainforest, with a national park inside it, far from the busy capital.
scenes.headline: Rainforest Half

scenes.narration: For years, driving between the two halves meant leaving Brunei, entering Malaysia, then crossing back into Brunei.
scenes.headline: Leave Your Country

scenes.narration: Then you did it all again on the way home. Four immigration checkpoints on that road, with passport stamps.
scenes.headline: Four Checkpoints

scenes.narration: In 2020, Brunei opened a bridge about thirty kilometres long, the longest in Southeast Asia, to skip Malaysia completely.
scenes.headline: The Giant Bridge

scenes.narration: Brunei is rich from oil and gas, which is why it can afford the kind of bridge most countries only dream about.
scenes.headline: Oil Pays For It

scenes.narration: So the bridge exists because of the split. A country built a giant bridge just to avoid crossing a neighbour.
scenes.headline: A Bridge To Avoid Malaysia

scenes.narration: Number six. Picture a country shaped like a finger poked deep into another country. That is The Gambia.
scenes.headline: The Gambia

scenes.narration: It is a thin strip of land, only about twenty-five to fifty kilometres wide, running along a river.
scenes.headline: A Thin Ribbon

scenes.narration: Senegal surrounds it on every side except the sea. Walk out from the river in any direction, and you reach Senegal.
scenes.headline: Senegal On All Sides

scenes.narration: Its capital, Banjul, sits where the Gambia River meets the Atlantic Ocean, at the very edge of the strip.
scenes.headline: Banjul, At The Coast

scenes.narration: Take the ferry across the river at Banjul and you are still in The Gambia, with Senegal close on both sides.
scenes.headline: Cross The River

scenes.narration: The country follows the river for hundreds of kilometres inland, and nowhere is it very wide.
scenes.headline: Hundreds Of Kilometres Long

scenes.narration: It is the smallest country on mainland Africa, yet it has its own flag, its own money and its own government.
scenes.headline: Smallest On Mainland

scenes.narration: The shape comes from colonial history, when Britain held the river and France held the land all around it.
scenes.headline: Britain And France

scenes.narration: So the border follows a river, not people, and the result is a country that looks like a ribbon.
scenes.headline: A Border By River

scenes.narration: Next, a piece of land that touches three countries, but not the one it belongs to.
scenes.headline: Up Next

scenes.narration: Number five. Nakhchivan belongs to Azerbaijan, but you cannot drive there from the rest of Azerbaijan.
scenes.headline: Nakhchivan

scenes.narration: Armenia sits right in the way. That makes Nakhchivan an exclave: a piece of a country sitting alone.
scenes.headline: An Exclave

scenes.narration: It touches Armenia, Iran and Turkey, but not a single kilometre of the rest of Azerbaijan.
scenes.headline: Three Neighbours

scenes.narration: On the map, it looks like a puzzle piece that fell off the main picture and landed somewhere else.
scenes.headline: A Fallen Puzzle Piece

scenes.narration: The lines come from the early Soviet years, when borders were drawn inside one big country.
scenes.headline: Soviet Lines

scenes.narration: When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991, those inside lines became real international borders, and Nakhchivan was stuck.
scenes.headline: Lines Become Borders

scenes.narration: It has its own parliament inside Azerbaijan. But travellers have often had to fly, or take a detour through Iran.
scenes.headline: Fly Or Detour

scenes.narration: Next is in Africa: an oil-rich region cut off from its own country by a thin strip of land.
scenes.headline: Next: Oil And A Strip

scenes.narration: Number four. Cabinda is part of Angola, but a strip of DR Congo separates it from the rest of Angola.
scenes.headline: Cabinda, Angola

scenes.narration: That strip runs along the mouth of the Congo River, and it gives DR Congo a small bit of Atlantic coast.
scenes.headline: Congo's Tiny Coast

scenes.narration: So Angola is split on the map, with Cabinda in the north and the main country far below.
scenes.headline: Angola In Two

scenes.narration: Cabinda is rich in oil, and a big share of Angola's oil has come from the waters off its coast.
scenes.headline: Oil Off The Coast

scenes.narration: Its status comes from a colonial past, when Portugal ruled Cabinda as a separate territory from the rest of Angola.
scenes.headline: A Separate Territory

scenes.narration: Cabinda also has a separatist movement that has existed for decades, so its odd shape matches a political struggle.
scenes.headline: A Long Struggle

scenes.narration: To go by road from Cabinda to the rest of Angola, you must pass through DR Congo and cross borders.
scenes.headline: Road Through Congo

scenes.narration: So you leave Angola, enter another country, and come back, just to travel inside your own.
scenes.headline: Leave To Stay Home

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places and facts that sound fake but are true, do subscribe. There is more on the way.
scenes.headline: Enjoying This?

scenes.narration: We are past halfway, and the next three get stranger. One of them is on India's own border.
scenes.headline: India Is Next

scenes.narration: Number three. On the island of Timor, Oecusse belongs to East Timor, but sits inside Indonesian West Timor.
scenes.headline: Oecusse

scenes.narration: East Timor, also called Timor-Leste, is a small country that holds the eastern half of the island.
scenes.headline: Half An Island

scenes.narration: Oecusse is a pocket on the northern coast, with Indonesia on its land sides and sea on the other.
scenes.headline: A Coastal Pocket

scenes.narration: To reach it from the East Timor capital, Dili, you either cross Indonesia, or take a boat or a plane.
scenes.headline: Cross, Sail Or Fly

scenes.narration: On the ground, a gate and guards mark where East Timor ends and Indonesia begins.
scenes.headline: A Gate On Timor

scenes.narration: Portugal landed here centuries ago, and Lifau, in Oecusse, became the first Portuguese capital on the island of Timor.
scenes.headline: Portugal Landed Here

scenes.narration: So this pocket is a leftover of old colonial claims, still sitting on today's map.
scenes.headline: A Colonial Leftover

scenes.narration: Imagine a small piece of Goa sitting inside Tamil Nadu, but still belonging to Goa. That is the idea.
scenes.headline: Goa Inside Tamil Nadu?

scenes.narration: Today, Oecusse is a special region with its own rules, meant to attract investment.
scenes.headline: A Special Region

scenes.narration: Now the last two are in India itself. And the final one has a gate with a timetable.
scenes.headline: A Gate With A Clock

scenes.narration: Number two. Dahagram and Angarpota are villages that belong to Bangladesh, but sit inside India.
scenes.headline: Dahagram-Angarpota

scenes.narration: They lie in West Bengal, near Cooch Behar, with Indian land on every side. That makes them an enclave.
scenes.headline: Near Cooch Behar

scenes.narration: An enclave is a piece of one country completely surrounded by another country.
scenes.headline: What Is An Enclave?

scenes.narration: For decades, this border was a puzzle of Indian and Bangladeshi villages mixed together like pieces of two different jigsaws.
scenes.headline: A Mixed-Up Border

scenes.narration: In 2015, India and Bangladesh swapped most of those enclaves, and thousands of people chose which country to live in.
scenes.headline: The 2015 Swap

scenes.narration: But Dahagram and Angarpota stayed Bangladeshi, because they already had a link back to the rest of Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Still Bangladeshi

scenes.narration: The people there are Bangladeshi citizens, but every road around their homes leads into India.
scenes.headline: Home Surrounded

scenes.narration: Just across the corridor lies Patgram, in Bangladesh's Lalmonirhat district, their nearest piece of mainland Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Mainland Is Close

scenes.narration: So how do they get to their own country? Through a small gift of land from India.
scenes.headline: A Gift Of Land

scenes.narration: That gift of land is number one, and it is the strangest border in India.
scenes.headline: The Strangest One

scenes.narration: Number one. The Tin Bigha Corridor, a small strip of Indian land leased to Bangladesh.
scenes.headline: Tin Bigha Corridor

scenes.narration: It measures about 178 metres by 85 metres, shorter than two football pitches laid end to end.
scenes.headline: Tiny Strip Of Land

scenes.narration: India leased it in perpetuity, under a 1974 agreement, so Bangladeshis can reach Dahagram and Angarpota.
scenes.headline: Leased Forever

scenes.narration: The land is still India's. But the people walking across it are Bangladeshi citizens, going home.
scenes.headline: Indian Land, Bangladeshi Feet

scenes.narration: Even with an agreement in 1974, the corridor only opened on the twenty-sixth of June, 1992.
scenes.headline: Opened In 1992

scenes.narration: And there is a gate. For years, guards opened it only at set times, around an hour at a time.
scenes.headline: A Gate On A Timetable

scenes.narration: Miss your slot, and you waited at the gate until the next opening. Imagine a road with a timetable.
scenes.headline: Miss Your Slot

scenes.narration: Each time the gate opens, people from Dahagram walk through Indian land to Bangladesh, and walk back again.
scenes.headline: The Gate Opens

scenes.narration: In 2011, the two countries agreed to keep it open round the clock, which made life easier for the villagers.
scenes.headline: Open Round The Clock

scenes.narration: Even now, it is a strip of Indian soil, with a gate and border guards, used by citizens of another country.
scenes.headline: Still A Border

scenes.narration: A door, a gate and a lane, built in the middle of India so strangers can walk home.
scenes.headline: A Lane To Walk Home

scenes.narration: Now go back to the hook. Crossing Malaysia twice, with passport stamps, just to reach your own country in Brunei.
scenes.headline: Back To Brunei

scenes.narration: Seven maps, seven odd shapes, and every one of them is true. The map in your head is never the full story.
scenes.headline: All Seven Are True

scenes.narration: Next time you look at a map, remember: some lines go around corners, through villages, and even through a gate.
scenes.headline: Lines Are Strange

scenes.narration: Next video: another place on the map that should not exist. Come and see it.
scenes.headline: Next Video
scenes.sub: A place that should not exist
